doc.title: Ellen Rowe interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 2, 2024

title: Writing by hand and thinking about the players
summary: Hand-written scores yield voicings tried at the piano and parts that are fun to play, a lineage from Rayburn Wright.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah, this again is another subject I’m passionate about and I’ll talk for hours — I’ll promise not to but I could. Yeah. I find, I can tell a difference between a student who has entered some big band score just on their computer, and a student who has taken the time to really sit down and try voicings and things out at the piano and done it by hand. Yeah it’s so important for me to think about the players who are playing the parts as I’m you know putting them out, and I’m really trying to think linearly — I’m not pronouncing that well but you know what I mean, as opposed, no, in addition to vertically. And I think that’s actually the nicest compliments I’ve ever gotten are from players who say hey I really enjoyed playing your music, you know because the parts were fun to play is generally what they’re getting at. So I think that a lot of that comes from the pencil and the paper. And I just feel more ownership, I feel closer to it and you know of course Dave studied with Rayburn Wright as well so we’re all cut from the same cloth.
